newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - US June industrial output up 0.3 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - US June industrial output up 0.3 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Federal Reserve said June industrial production rose 0.3 percent against a revised 0.2-percent rise in May. Capacity utilization was unchanged at 83.5 percent.
Economists in a Reuters survey had expected a 0.2-percent rise in June industrial output, and capacity utilization of 83.6 percent.
CHRISTOPHER RUPKEY, ECONOMIST, BANK OF TOKYO-MITSUBISHI:
"I think it's pretty much neutral. It is the Fed's own number and they have made policy changes off it in the past."
Rupkey, who was speaking on Reuters Financial Television, said he expected a Fed rate hike perhaps later in the third quarter.
CHARLES LIEBERMAN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CHASE SECURITIES INC:

"(The 0.3-percent rise in industrial production in June) was exactly our forecast. Capacity use was unchanged. And May industrial production was revised slightly lower to 0.2 percent from 0.4 percent. I would call the report basically in line with expectations. It shows moderate growth; respectable, moderate growth.

"It should have relatively little impact on the (Treasury) market. The market knows that inflation is well behaved and growth has moderated and that's exactly the message of these two reports. There really are no surprises.
"The question is can the market go higher with more of the kind of data that we've gotten. And I think the answer is it really needs something more to push it higher," he added.
JOSH FEINMAN, GLOBAL MARKETS ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST CO:
"Industrial production in June looks broadly in line with expectations, although it may be a tad stronger than expected.
"But we had a (two-tenths of a percentage point) downward revision in May. When you put it all together it's basically in line with expectations.

"Capacity utilitzation is also about as expected and suggests that there is not all that much strain in the industrial sector. There is nothing in here to get in the way of the market feeling that the Federal Reserve is on hold and the good times can continue," Feinman concluded.
CHERYL KATZ, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH & CO INC: "It came in line with expectations.

"The manuafacturing sector is growing at a moderate and sustainable rate with manufacturing capacity growing at a 4.2-percent year-over-year rate. There continues to be almost a complete lack of bottleneck pressures.
"This is quite bullish for inflation.
"At the beginning of the year you did start to see production getting ahead of demand, perhaps now the manufacturing sector is returning to a more sustainable pace."

CHRIS IGGO, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BZW SECURITIES INC: The only standout was "auto production bounced back a bit after strike action in April and May. Everything else looks pretty moderate. There was something of a deceleration in industrial production overall."

Looking forward, "It's hard to say" how long this trend can persist, he said. But, "industrial production really lags demand. What we've seen in recent months is demand slowing, particularly consumer demand." That portends "sluggishness in the third quarter as well," Iggo said.

RAM BHAGAVATULA, CHIEF FINANCIAL ECONOMIST, CITICORP GLOBAL FINANCE N.A.: "The industrial production report is about as expected. There are no surprises. They revised May down a touch, which is appropriate because we thought the May number looked high.
"We don't see any capacity pressures building. Capacity utilization is about where it's been for a whole year now.

"The data presents a picture of moderate economic growth and to the extent that the present growth rate is not putting a whole lot of pressure on capacity use, that means the inflation outlook remains reasonably benign, which means that financial asset prices should do all right."

TIMOTHY MARTIN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NATIONSBANK CORP: "When taking into account May's downward revision, the June industrial production data were a little bit on the soft side. The bond market will react favorably to it. Overall, production is not accelerating. However, in the June report auto production was strong. Certainly with the slowdown in car sales, that won't continue.
"High tech equipment is still strong and so is regular business equipment. But weaker consumer spending looks like it will affect consumer durable goods, especially cars."
ASTRID ADOLFSON, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MCM MONEYWATCH INC:
"The (production) data were pretty much as expercted. A little bit softer, but that is in line with what we saw in the (June) labor report.
"If you take into account the strike-related rebound, the auto, the high-tech and the aircraft were ... the strongest parts of the report. The rest was a bit softer.

"(Fed Chairman Alan) Greenspan can now go before Congress next week and say that the economy has slowed to trend, but there is no sign of deceleration and he can wait to see if the economy chugs along at a faster-than-trend level."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660 ))
